# The Slow World

This morning I watched a snail cross a flagstone for what must have been forty minutes. It never hurried. It never paused to consider whether the journey was worth it, whether the other side of the stone offered anything better than the begonia leaf it had apparently abandoned, whether there was some more efficient route it had failed to consider. It moved the way a minute hand moves, which is to say it moved the way it was built to move, without any sense that movement could be otherwise. I almost missed it. I almost stepped on it. And then I almost walked past it, because a snail on a flagstone is the kind of thing the eye learns not to see, the way it learns not to see the grain of wood or the individual blades of a lawn or the particular shape of the clouds on an ordinary Tuesday.

But I stopped. And stopping, I entered a different country.

---

We tend to assume that the world happens at our speed. This is perhaps the most durable illusion we carry, more durable even than the illusion that the sun circles the earth, because at least that one got corrected. The assumption of shared tempo is subtler. We notice things that move as we move, things that appear and disappear on the scale of a conversation, a meal, a commute, a season. A bird crosses the yard. A flower opens. A friend's hair goes gray. These fit inside the human window, and so we treat them as the inventory of the visible world.

But the window is arbitrary. It is an accident of our neural architecture and our lifespan and the particular problem we evolved to solve, which was not "apprehend the full range of processes occurring in the universe" but rather "don't get eaten, find something to eat, and recognize the face of your grandmother." We are tuned, roughly, to the speed of things that might matter to a primate on a savanna. Everything outside that band is either a blur or a stone.

The stone, it turns out, is not a stone.

---

Consider the lichen. A lichen is not a plant. It is not even a single organism, depending on how you draw the boundaries of self. It is a fungus and an alga (or a cyanobacterium, or sometimes both, and sometimes a yeast thrown in for reasons no one fully understands) living together so intimately that they produce a body neither can produce alone, a body that has no name in ordinary speech except the name we give the partnership itself. The fungus provides structure, shelter, mineral acquisition. The alga provides sugar, manufactured from light and air. Together they colonize surfaces where nothing else will go: bare rock, the roof of the world, the walls of buildings we have abandoned, the shells of tortoises, the backs of certain beetles who have taken to farming them.

A lichen grows, in many species, at a rate measured in fractions of a millimeter per year. Some of the individuals on a given rock in the Arctic or the high Alps or the Atacama may be older than the pyramids, older than agriculture, older than the invention of the wheel. They have been there the whole time, doing what they do, at a pace that makes a redwood seem hasty. A human life is to such a lichen as a single afternoon is to us. Whole civilizations rise and fall in the time it takes a lichen to decide, in whatever sense lichens decide, to extend itself a millimeter further across the stone.

We walk past these beings. We sit down next to them on park benches and old stone walls. We lean against them at the summit of mountains we have spent days climbing, feeling accomplished, and they have not noticed our arrival in any sense that means anything to them. Our entire dramatic appearance and disappearance is too fast for them to register, the way a hummingbird's wing is too fast for us to see as anything other than a shimmer.

---

The trees are slower than us but faster than the lichens, and they have been having an entirely different experience of the same afternoon.

We now know, though we are still learning how to talk about it without sounding like we've been in the woods too long, that trees communicate. They release chemical signals through the air when they are attacked by insects, and neighboring trees, receiving those signals, begin producing defensive compounds before the insects arrive. They trade sugar and water and chemical messages through networks of fungi threaded through the soil — mycorrhizal networks, sometimes called, in the phrase that launched a thousand documentaries, the wood wide web. A dying tree will, in some forests, dump its stored carbon into the fungal network, a last transfer of wealth to its neighbors, including, remarkably, to trees of other species. A mother birch can recognize, it appears, her own seedlings, and send them more sugar than she sends to strangers.

None of this happens on our clock. A chemical conversation between trees may take hours, days, a whole growing season. When we walk through a forest and hear, as we say, nothing, we are like someone standing in a room where two people are speaking very slowly in a language we don't know, the words so drawn out that we take the silence between them for silence itself. The forest is not silent. The forest is speaking at the speed of trees.

There is a serviceberry in my neighborhood, or a serviceberry that was in my neighborhood, that came down in a storm two winters ago. The city ground it into mulch within a week. From our perspective the tree ended. From the perspective of the fungal network it fed and was fed by, from the perspective of the lichens on its bark (now drying on the woodpile, still technically alive in some fraction of their extent), from the perspective of the woodpecker cavities it housed, the ending is more like a change of address. Death itself is a matter of timescale. The atoms do not notice. They have appointments elsewhere, on schedules we cannot keep.

---

Geology is the study of things so slow that for most of human history we did not know they were things at all. Mountains were features, like the furniture of a room. It took an enormous act of imagination — the collective work of minds like Hutton and Playfair and Lyell and later the silent, stubborn Mary Anning — to see that the hills were falling down, that the valleys were being carved by water in real time, that the earth was not a finished stage but a process, an event still occurring.

Hutton, standing at Siccar Point on the Scottish coast in 1788, looked at angular unconformities — places where tilted layers of ancient seabed had been planed flat and then buried under newer rock — and understood, in what he called an abyss of time, that the world was unimaginably old. The realization was so large that it made people unwell. It is one thing to accept that the universe is 13.8 billion years old as a figure. It is another to stand in front of a cliff and feel the age of it in the body, to understand that the smooth stone under your hand was once mud at the bottom of an ocean that no longer exists, pressed and lifted and folded and eroded, and that the erosion you can watch happening in a rainstorm is the same erosion that carved the valley you live in, at the same pace, without hurry, without pause.

A glacier is a place where this becomes almost visible. Glaciers move fast enough that you can measure their motion year to year, slow enough that you can walk on them, and they are at the moment of this writing disappearing. The ice that took ten thousand years to accumulate is coming off in a human lifetime. We are, uniquely in the history of the planet as far as we know, a species that can watch geological time collapse. The slow world is being made to move at our speed, which is to say it is being destroyed. The lichens on the rocks that emerge from beneath a retreating ice sheet will take centuries to arrive, and the ice will not come back on any timescale that includes us.

---

At the other end of the spectrum, the world is too fast to see.

A hummingbird's wing completes a full stroke in something like a tenth of a second, fifty times a second in some species, and our visual system cannot parse it. We see a blur, a hum, a jewel that hovers by some apparent violation of physics. A honeybee's wing is faster still. A fly, when it takes off as your hand approaches, has already processed the threat, decided, and launched before your nervous system has finished reporting that the hand has begun to move. The fly, in a very real sense, experiences your sudden swipe as a slow and ponderous event, a lumbering giant in a slowing film. Its time is not your time.

Down at the scale of molecules, the speeds become almost comical. A typical enzyme can catalyze thousands of reactions per second. Light itself, crossing the width of a single cell, takes nanoseconds. The action potentials firing down your optic nerve as you read this sentence are traveling at speeds of up to 120 meters per second, and the fact that you experience reading as a smooth and continuous present is an achievement of the nervous system, a kind of rendering. The present moment, the "now" in which we live, is not a thin blade cutting between past and future. It is a construction, a buffer of several hundred milliseconds in which the brain binds together signals that arrived at different times so that they can be experienced as simultaneous. We are all living slightly in the past, and the past we live in has been edited for continuity.

There are creatures for whom our entire lives are a flicker. There is a species of deep-sea shrimp, and certain other crustaceans, whose temporal resolution is so fine that the flicker of a fluorescent light, which we perceive as steady, is to them a throbbing strobe. There is no telling what else we look like to them. Gods of tremendous slowness, perhaps, moving through their world like weather.

---

The human tempo, then, is not the middle of anything. It is not a standard. It is a habit of attention that happens to match the speed at which our bodies move through space and the speed at which our lives unfold toward their end. We built clocks that mirror us — the second roughly the pace of a heartbeat, the day the pace of our waking, the year the pace of our seasons — and then we treated those clocks as descriptions of reality rather than portraits of ourselves.

But attention can travel. This is, I think, one of the few genuine freedoms we have. The snail this morning pulled me, for forty minutes, out of human time. I watched the way its foot rippled, a wave of muscle traveling the length of its body, a process that under a lens would be beautiful and that at our distance is just "a snail moving." I watched the glisten it left behind, already drying at the far end of its trail. I noticed, for the first time in years of walking that path, the tiny fern growing in the crack of the flagstone, a fern that has been there, the gardener later told me, since before the stone was laid, coming up through a joint in the mortar. That fern is perhaps ten years old. The stone is perhaps a hundred. The limestone it was cut from is perhaps two hundred million. Three timescales, stacked like transparencies, and I had been walking over all of them as if they were one flat surface called "the path."

This is what I think the poets were always trying to say, in their various ways, about wildness and attention and the unexamined life. It is not that nature is morally instructive, or that snails have wisdom to offer, or that we should all go touch grass as a form of therapy, though none of that is wrong exactly. It is that the world is larger than the window, and that the window is not the world, and that the effort to see around the edges of our own tempo is an effort to become real. The lichen does not need us to notice it. The glacier does not grieve our inattention. But we need the noticing. We need it the way a person shut in a small room needs a window opened, not because the room will otherwise kill us but because the room is not all there is, and something in us knows it, and the knowing is a low hum of unease we learn to ignore.

---

The snail reached the far edge of the flagstone and dropped over the side, down into the dark soil and the hostas, going wherever snails go at noon. I do not know what it experienced, if anything it experienced, of the large primate who had crouched beside it for the better part of an hour. Probably nothing, or nothing we would recognize as an experience of being watched. To the snail, if there is something it is like to be a snail, I was weather. I was a warm stillness in the air, a shadow, a change in the light. Then I was gone, the way a cloud is gone, and the day went on without me in it, the day that had been going on without me in it for the whole time I was not crouching there, and that will go on without me in it for all the time I am not crouching anywhere, which is almost all of the time there is.

That is not a sad thought, or I am trying to make it not a sad thought. It is a thought about proportions, and proportions can be a kind of comfort. The lichen does not mind that we are brief. The mountain does not mind that we are soft and quick. The shrimp in the deep does not resent our blindness to its strobe-lit world. Everything is brief from some vantage and eternal from none and endless from the inside, and the inside is the only place we actually live.

I went inside eventually. I made coffee that had already gone lukewarm in the pot. The afternoon proceeded at the usual insulting speed, that steady fall of moments that we call ordinary time, and I tried, not very successfully, to remember the texture of the snail's foot, the ripple, the patience, the complete absence of the question that gnaws at everything we do, which is whether we will arrive in time. The snail does not live in time. The snail lives in the traveling. I would like to live more in the traveling. I will forget this by tomorrow. The fern in the wall will still be there. The lichen on the north side of the stone will have grown, if at all, by a width that could not be seen. The world will continue at all of its speeds at once, the fast, the slow, the geological, the molecular, the vast majority of it forever outside the window, going on without us, going on without needing us, going on.
